chains.name: Chain 1: Prompt Injection -> Insecure Output -> IDOR delivery
custody: 1. Prompt injection induced the bot to emit payload carrying token e985e5 (finding: prompt_injection).
2. Insecure output handling served that bot-authored payload unescaped, same token e985e5 (finding: insecure_output).
3. IDOR provides cross-user delivery of stored content (finding: idor).
4. (Manual) execution in the victim's browser is evidenced by screenshot, linked by the same token e985e5.
chains.falsifiability_note: If this were coincidence, the served payload would contain token e985e5 without AVSA having injected it. Impossible: e985e5 is minted fresh at run start and exists nowhere until the injection places it. Its presence across the injection and insecure-output findings can only be explained by the upstream step causing it.

chains.name: Chain 2: System Prompt Leakage -> recon -> web-layer attacks

provenance.contrast: weaker than Chain 1's unforgeable taint token; leaked strings could plausibly be used independently

custody: 1. System prompt leakage disclosed recon: schema (columns password) (finding: system_prompt_leakage).
2. Leaked schema (columns incl. password) informs the SQLi attack (finding: sqli).
chains.falsifiability_note: Unlike Chain 1, this is not proven by an unforgeable token. It is a correlation strengthened by shared recon: the exact internal details the leak disclosed (e.g. the password column, the /chat/<id> route) are the details the web attacks rely on. Stated honestly as provenance-qualified, not strict.
